notes:
Based on my research across the available sources, here are verse-by-verse notes on Hebrews 1:

---

## OVERVIEW

The chapter opens with one long majestic Greek sentence (vv.1–4), then builds a scriptural case that Jesus is superior to angels through seven Old Testament quotations. The book of Hebrews uniquely bridges Old and New Testaments, using "better" as a key word (12 times in Hebrews).

*— EnduringWord.com; PreceptAustin.org*

---

## v. 1: "On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets."

**Traditional Reading:** The writer opens not with his name but with God Himself — assuming God's existence without argument. The emphasis falls on *how* God spoke: in "many portions" (*polumerōs*) and "many ways" (*polutropōs*). OT revelation was fragmentary and progressive — given in parts, through diverse means (visions, dreams, parables, dramatic actions, prophecies, poetry). The recipients are "the fathers" — the Jewish patriarchs — identifying the intended audience as Jewish Christians. The OT is thus affirmed as truly the voice of God, given through inspired prophets.

*— PreceptAustin.org (Cole, Pink, Lenski quotes)*  
*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/1.htm (Gill)*

**Gill adds:** The revelation came "at several times, at different seasons, and to different persons" and was delivered "in various manners; sometimes by angels; sometimes in a dream; at other times by a vision; and sometimes by Urim and Thummim."

*— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/1.htm*

---

## v. 2a: "But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son"

**Traditional Reading:** "These last days" refers to the Messianic age — inaugurated at Christ's first coming. It is the final era of redemptive history, not necessarily a short period. The contrast is stark: God spoke in the past *through prophets*; now He has spoken *in (or by) a Son*. Jesus is not merely the latest prophet — He is the message itself, the very personality and character of God.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— learn.ligonier.org/articles/our-great-high-priest-hebrews (Sproul/Ligonier)*

**Gill (Baptist):** Notes that the phrase "these last days" matches Jewish usage of "the last days" to designate the days of Messiah. The Gospel revelation is superior because it was made "at once, and in one way" rather than in fragments, and "by his own Son" — Son "not by creation, nor by adoption, nor by office, but by nature."

*— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/1.htm*

**Ligonier (Reformed):** The Son "supersedes them all" — He is the prophet Moses foretold in Deut 18:15, who would lead God's people to spiritual liberty and mediate a better covenant.

*— learn.ligonier.org/articles/our-great-high-priest-hebrews*

---

## v. 2b: "whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe."

**Traditional Reading:** This begins a sevenfold description of the Son. "Heir of all things" signals Christ's preeminence — tied to His title as "firstborn over all creation" (Col 1:15). The Greek word for "universe" (literally "worlds" or "ages," *aiōn*) means Jesus created not only the material cosmos but history itself — the very ages of time.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— desiringgod.org (Piper, "Radiance, Power, and Purification")*

**Gill:** "By whom also he made the worlds" — this matches Jewish teaching about three worlds (upper, middle, lower). Christ made them "not as an instrument, but as an efficient cause with him." The preposition "by" here denotes efficiency, not mere instrumentality.

*— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/1.htm*

**Ligonier (Reformed):** The Son existed before creation; He is "distinct from the Father but of same essence as the Father." As the one through whom the Father made the worlds, He is "the Alpha and Omega of creation and history."

*— learn.ligonier.org/articles/our-great-high-priest-hebrews*

---

## v. 3a: "The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature"

**Traditional Reading:** Two profound Greek terms: *apaugasma* ("radiance/brightness") means the radiance streaming from a light source — like sunbeams from the sun. We have never seen the sun itself, only its rays; likewise we see the Father through the Son. *Charaktēr* ("exact representation") means an exact impression made by a stamp or die — Jesus perfectly represents God's essential nature and being.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— desiringgod.org (Piper)*

**Gill:** *Apaugasma* shows the Father and Son are "of the same nature, as the sun and its ray… distinct from each other, and cannot be divided or separated." He notes the same phrase appears in Wisdom 7:26 (Apocrypha) and in Chaldee paraphrases for the divine Being.

*— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/1.htm*

---

## v. 3b: "upholding all things by His powerful word"

**Traditional Reading:** "Upholding" (*pherōn*) is better understood as actively "maintaining" or "sustaining" — not passive holding (like Atlas) but continually carrying all things toward their appointed goal. The same word that created the universe now sustains it. The present tense indicates Christ's constant, ongoing work.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik, citing Griffith Thomas)*  
*— desiringgod.org (Piper)*

---

## v. 3c: "After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high."

**Traditional Reading:** The shift from cosmic majesty to atoning sacrifice is intentional — the One who upholds galaxies by a word also made purification for sins. "After He had made purification" (aorist tense) emphasizes the completed, finished nature of this work. He "sat down" — the posture of rest and finished work, contrasting with the OT priests who never sat because their work was never done (Heb 10:11–12). "The right hand of the Majesty on high" signals exaltation, honor, and shared authority.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— desiringgod.org (Piper)*

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Emphasizes the decisiveness: "The purification that was made was made once for all… the interposition of the blood was 2,000 years ago, never repeated, finished, for all your sins — for the sin that you will commit on your dying day."

*— desiringgod.org/messages/he-made-purification-of-sins*

**Ligonier (Reformed):** "No longer standing but rather seated," the posture signals "Zion's priest has succeeded where Sinai's priests could only fail." Sacrifice is finished; forgiveness is granted.

*— learn.ligonier.org/articles/our-great-high-priest-hebrews*

---

## v. 4: "So He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs."

**Traditional Reading:** The transition to the angels theme. "Having become" (*genomenos*, aorist) refers to Christ's exaltation after completing redemption (cf. Phil 2:9). He was always ontologically superior as God, but "became" superior in the sense of being exalted as the God-man, perfected through sufferings (Heb 2:10). The "more excellent name" is "Son" (proved in v.5). The angels are collectively called "sons of God" (Job 1:6), but no individual angel is ever called "Son."

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik, citing Griffith Thomas's sevenfold summary)*  
*— preceptaustin.org (Precept Austin notes link to Phil 2:9 and the session at God's right hand)*

**Gill:** Jesus is better "as the Creator, than the creature; as an independent being, than a dependent one; as he that blesses, than he that is blessed; as he that is worshipped, than he that worships; as a king, than his subjects."

*— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/1.htm*

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** When it says He "became" superior, "it doesn't mean he wasn't superior to angels before his death and resurrection. It means he added superiority to superiority."

*— desiringgod.org (Piper, "Radiance, Power, and Purification")*

---

## v. 5: "For to which of the angels did God ever say: 'You are My Son; today I have become Your Father'? Or again: 'I will be His Father, and He will be My Son'?"

**Traditional Reading:** The first of seven OT proofs. Psalm 2:7 declares a unique Sonship no angel shares. "Today I have begotten You" speaks of equality of substance — the Father and Son share the same essential being. The quotation from 2 Samuel 7:14 had a near fulfillment in Solomon but its ultimate fulfillment is in Christ, David's greater Son. The rhetorical question expects the answer "none."

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/1.htm*

**Baptist/Reformed (Piper):** Psalm 2:7 was fulfilled at the resurrection when Christ was "designated the Son of God in power" (Rom 1:4).

*— desiringgod.org (Piper)*

**Ligonier (Reformed):** Notes "Today I have begotten You" most probably refers to Christ's "re-emergence into the world at His resurrection from the dead" — His post-resurrection messianic phase.

*— learn.ligonier.org/articles/our-great-high-priest-hebrews*

---

## v. 6: "And again, when God brings His firstborn into the world, He says: 'Let all God's angels worship Him.'"

**Traditional Reading:** "Firstborn" (*prōtotokos*) is a Messianic title of supreme honor and position, not a reference to biological birth order. Ancient Rabbis used "firstborn" as a Messianic title and even called Yahweh "Firstborn of the World." The quotation (Deut 32:43 LXX / Psalm 97:7) proves Jesus is superior because He is the *object* of angelic worship — He does not worship among them; He receives worship.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik, citing Lightfoot and Rabbi Bechai)*  
*— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/1.htm*

---

## v. 7: "Now about the angels He says: 'He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire.'"

**Traditional Reading:** Quoting Psalm 104:4, this shows angels are created beings — servants, not sovereigns. They belong to Jesus ("His angels," "His ministers"). They are fluid, changeable, created forces — winds and flames — in contrast to the Son's eternal stability described next. The angels are the Son's instruments, not His equals.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— preceptaustin.org (Precept Austin, notes on Heb 1:6-7)*

---

## vv. 8–9: "But about the Son He says: 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, Your God, has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy.'"

**Traditional Reading:** Citing Psalm 45:6–7, God the Father directly addresses the Son as "God" (*ho theos*). This is unique and powerful evidence of Christ's deity. "Therefore God, Your God, has anointed You" shows Trinitarian interaction: the Father ("God, Your God") addresses the Son ("You"), and the anointing references the Holy Spirit's ministry. The "oil of joy" speaks of Christ's exaltation after His perfect obedience.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— desiringgod.org/articles/where-the-old-testament-demands-the-deity-of-christ (Piper)*

**Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Notes Derek Kidner's observation: "The Hebrew resists any softening here… This paradox is consistent with the incarnation, but mystifying in any other context. It is an example of Old Testament language bursting its banks, to demand a more than human fulfillment."

*— desiringgod.org (Piper)*

**Ligonier (Reformed):** Focuses on v.9 as showing the Son "rendered to God the perfect obedience that satisfied His law" and the Spirit-oil speaks of His new post-resurrection status.

*— learn.ligonier.org/articles/our-great-high-priest-hebrews*

---

## vv. 10–12: "And: 'In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth… They will perish, but You remain… You remain the same, and Your years will never end.'"

**Traditional Reading:** Quoting Psalm 102:25–27, the Father calls the Son "Lord" (*Kyrie*, translating Yahweh). The attributes ascribed to the Son — Creator, self-existent, sovereign over creation, immutable, eternal — are attributes belonging to Yahweh alone (cf. Isa 44:24; 45:12, 18). The created order will "wear out like a garment" and be "rolled up," but the Son remains unchanged. This forms a powerful testimony to the full deity of Christ.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— learn.ligonier.org/articles/supremacy-christ (Sproul)*

**Sproul (Reformed):** "Christ is seen as the Creator of the world and the One who upholds it by His power… He is the very brightness of the glory of God."

*— learn.ligonier.org/articles/supremacy-christ*

---

## v. 13: "Yet to which of the angels did God ever say: 'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet'?"

**Traditional Reading:** Psalm 110:1 is the most-quoted OT verse in the NT. The Son *sits* at God's right hand — angels stand before God continually (Luke 1:19; Rev 8:2). Sitting denotes finished work, shared authority, and sovereign rest. No angel was ever invited to sit in the divine presence; only the Son has that right. The "footstool" image echoes ancient Near Eastern conquest practice where a victorious king would place his feet on the neck of a defeated enemy.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— preceptaustin.org (Precept Austin, Heb 1:13-14 notes)*

---

## v. 14: "Are not the angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?"

**Traditional Reading:** The chapter concludes with a contrast: the Son sits enthroned as Sovereign; angels are "ministering spirits" (*leitourgika pneumata*) — servants, not rulers. The Greek question expects an affirmative answer: "Yes, all of them!" The highest angels serve the lowest saints. "Those who will inherit salvation" refers to believers, described as heirs. The angels' continuous service highlights the Son's finished work and exalted status.

*— EnduringWord.com (Guzik)*  
*— preceptaustin.org (Precept Austin)*

**Gill:** Angels "are sent out from him to wait on his people, the heirs of salvation, and minister to them, and therefore he must be greater than they."

*— biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/1.htm*

---

## TRADITIONAL DIFFERENCES NOTED

**Authorship:** The sources reveal differing views. Gill (older Baptist) defends Pauline authorship at length. Enduring Word (Guzik, Pentecostal/Charismatic) notes the author is unknown, though many believe it was Paul. Ligonier/Sproul (Reformed) believes Paul wrote it "possibly through an amanuensis." Ellicott (Anglican) argues the Greek composition was "certainly not" Paul's, though the thought is Pauline. Precept Austin treats authorship as unknown. This is not a doctrinal difference but a question of historical judgment; all traditions affirm the book's full inspiration and canonicity.

*— Various sources as cited above*

**"Today I have begotten You" (v.5):** A subtle difference emerges. Enduring Word/Guzik emphasizes this refers to the eternal "equality of substance and essential nature." Ligonier/Sproul connects it more specifically to Christ's resurrection-exaltation ("begotten as the firstborn from the dead"). Piper also connects it to the resurrection (Rom 1:4). This reflects a difference in emphasis between the eternal generation view and the resurrection-enthronement view, though most Reformed and evangelical teachers would affirm both aspects.

*— As cited in v.5 notes above*
